articles.title: York Uni students' fears over Turnitin essay-checker AI plan
articles.summary: Students are "scared" about proposals which could see their work used to train AI, their union says.
articles.body:
University students have raised concerns over the software used to submit assignments and check them for plagiarism, amid fears their work could be used to train tools which use artificial intelligence.

The University of York Students' Union said planned changes to the licence agreement for the Turnitin system could see students' work used to teach AI models.

The University of York has said it would review any changes to the software's terms and conditions, while the University of Southampton has already started to phase out the system.

A spokesperson for Turnitin said its policy would not be updated any earlier than September 2027 to "give us time to discuss any changes with customers".

The tools which have caused concern use machine learning to compare students' work to other submissions and existing academic articles in an effort to identify potential plagiarism, but they do not reproduce or write students' work.

Sam Dickinson, union affairs officer at York Students' Union, said students' concerns were raised in August before Turnitin announced that any changes would not take place at least until September next year.

"The key issue here is that students' intellectual property is something that should belong to them," he explained.

"I think there's a fear when AI policies are introduced like this that their work is going to be whisked away and used for something other than student progress at university."

Dickinson said a falling number of graduate job vacancies, partly attributed to AI, contributed to "massive anxiety" among students.

Meanwhile, they were also concerned "more broadly that AI is being used to train services without the meaningful consent of the people who created that content".

"If your university is using Turnitin and it's using student-submitted work to train AI services, you can't meaningfully consent to that because you have to submit your work to get marked," he said.

"If you're at university, if you're writing about things you really, really care about, you should own that work and be able to decide whether it's used to train AI services."

In a statement, a spokesperson for the California-based tech firm said: "As Turnitin has expanded the in-product use of AI, and as we assist customers in navigating their own AI use, our institutional agreements were updated to reflect current data practices.

"To give us time to discuss any changes with customers, we are not updating it any earlier than September 1, 2027.

"We do not use customer or student work to train the AI assistant within Turnitin Clarity.

"We may use anonymized student submissions to improve our detection and assessment tools."

A spokesperson for the University of York said Turnitin had been contact and the university understood that "no changes will be made to our terms and conditions, and our students' data will not be used to train their AI services".

"Safeguarding intellectual property and data privacy are really important to us," they said.

"If such a provider changes their terms and conditions, this is something we would review, and we are meeting with the Students' Union to discuss the issues raised."

According to the website Uni Compare, 98% of UK universities used Turnitin products.

However, the University of Southampton has said it would be "phasing out the use of this service immediately" and would not renew its contract with Turnitin after the 2026-27 academic year.

A spokesperson for the university said: "We have a responsibility to protect the data, intellectual property and academic work of our students and the university.

"While we understand Turnitin has postponed changes to the end-user licence agreement that would have allowed it to use student submissions to train AI services, it has not fully clarified what future changes may be imposed."

The spokesperson added that other options were being evaluated "to ensure that academic integrity standards are maintained".

Students' Union presidents at the University of Reading have said they were "aware of students' concerns" about the proposed changes to the licence agreements for Turnitin.

In a statement on Instagram, they said they would "ask what the university's plans are, how it intends to protect students' interests and what any future changes could mean for submitting assessments".

Meanwhile, the undergraduate education officer at the University of East Anglia Students' Union said they had held "positive discussions" with uni bosses about Turnitin.

"There is strong inclination from both sides to move away from the usage of the service with Turnitin's change in terms and conditions and for smoother university operation," they added.

At Lancaster University, Students' Union education officer Niamh McAuley said in a video on social media that she was due to hold discussions with the university with the aim of stopping students' work being used to train AI.

She told students: "Your work should belong to you and you should fundamentally make decisions whether it's being used."

Emily Bannister, St Andrews University's SU president for education, said the proposed policy change was a "fundamental challenge to the principles of academic integrity" .

She said she had written to Turnitin's CEO and the university's leadership team, with "positive engagement" so far.

articles.title: Food banks 'in crisis' as some face threat of closure in Northern Ireland
articles.summary: According to the Trussell Trust, an anti-poverty charity, some food banks are having pay for 30-50% of the food they are supplying.
articles.body:
The manager of a food bank in County Fermanagh has said they have enough money for "two months of running costs" before they run out, while another in west Belfast has had to "significantly reduce" the sizes of their parcels.

According to the Trussell Trust, an anti-poverty charity, some food banks are having pay for 30-50% of the food they are supplying.

Enniskillen Foodbank said their ongoing expenses were continuing and donations were "not keeping pace" with project manager Paul Dickson describing it as it a "bleak situation".

Edel Diamond from South West Belfast Foodbank on the Stewartstown Road said they were struggling with stock which was "really upsetting because you've got families coming to you that aren't really coping".

Enniskillen Foodbank is part of the Trussell Trust network which can provide support for another three months.

"That isn't enough to last a year," Dickson told Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme.

"It's brilliant to get that [support from the trust] but...we need to create network of relationships locally that help make food banks sustainable."

He added that he noticed a drop in donations given to supermarkets but understood that things were becoming more expensive.

"Part of the Trussell ethos is that we don't believe that we should be needed, but unfortunately, we are needed at the minute and we need to be here for the people that rely on us."

'We are in crisis' as parcel sizes are reduced

Diamond, from the South West Belfast Foodbank, said that while she was thankful they were not having to turn people away, it was distressing.

"It seems to me like one cost-of-living crisis is just rolling into another and it doesn't seem to have gone away," she said.

She added that rising energy costs had a knock-on effect on charities.

"We're not just a food bank, we are places of comfort for people, places where people can come and find that hope," Diamond said.

"We want to see the end for the need for food banks, but at this immediate time we are in crisis and we're urgently appealing for donations of food and finance."

Fiona Cole, from Trussell Trust in Northern Ireland, said it was "heartbreaking" to see food banks in this situation, adding the stress on food bank managers and volunteers is increasing on a daily basis.

According to the Trussell Trust, 67,851 parcels were distributed in Northern Ireland, 26,459 of those given to children in 2025.

The policy and public affairs manager said in the last four to six weeks, food banks had faced a crisis in terms of stock levels.

"Our biggest fear is that our food banks are prematurely forced to drastically reduce their support, or worse, close their doors because the income they receive falls short and they can no longer afford their household essentials," Cole said.

She said that fewer donations could be a result of people struggling with cost of living and having to cut their own budgets.

"Our lifelong contributors, they would give us £5 of food or £10 of food every time they go to shop in a supermarket," Cole said.

"That £10 of food is just simply not the same amount as what you would have got even six months ago."

She said three food banks had contacted them directly about concerns with stock and finance, and six in total had to put out emergency appeals for donations on social media.

She added food banks had also had to close distribution centres or reduce their hours.

Cole said there needed to be sustainable funding for food banks to operate as well as support from government and the Northern Assembly.

While food banks are under pressure a Trussell Trust report found that they had been distributing fewer parcels in 2025 than the peak seen in 2023.

"Wider data suggests there has been a corresponding fall in need for food banks, not just use ".

articles.title: Corrie Mckeague's mum: 'I've given myself closure; my son's dead'
articles.summary: Nicola Urquhart speaks to the BBC on the 10th anniversary of her 23-year-old son's disappearance.
articles.body:
"We definitely did all we could and I can honestly sleep at night knowing there was nothing I physically could have done any different."

It is 10 years since Nicola Urquhart's son, Corrie Mckeague, disappeared on 24 September 2016 after a night out in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk. For the months and years that followed, she embodied a mother's love and determination to find the truth: to never give up.

The RAF gunner's body has never been found but he was officially declared dead in 2022, when an inquest ruled he had died after climbing into a commercial waste bin before it was tipped into a waste lorry.

Nicola is composed and reflective as she recalls when her son went missing. He had just turned 23 and within months would become a dad.

She says her son would be forever in her thoughts, but adds: "I've given myself closure; my son is dead."

She spoke to the BBC after what would have been Corrie's 33rd birthday and ahead of the 10th anniversary of his disappearance.

She says she last saw her son when she went for a birthday meal with him at Cheers in Bury St Edmunds, adding he was a "social hand grenade" who "really did live every moment at a hundred miles an hour".

A decade on, she says there is "never an end" to losing somebody but it is about "managing each day".

'The anniversary is difficult but we try to be positive'

"Every time I drive up a road, as I'm driving I still look at the verges, I can't stop myself," says Nicola.

"The anniversary is difficult, but we will still try to be positive about it and the universe makes us remember it and generally in a really nice way.

"We are fine, but that is a conscious, deliberate effort to be fine because it would be a disservice to his memory if we just shut down and didn't make the best of our lives.

"In every single way that you can think, there is not one day, one decision, that doesn't go by without Corrie being at the forefront of it," she adds.

Airman Corrie, who was based at RAF Honington in Suffolk, had enjoyed a night out drinking when he was thrown out of a nightclub and became separated from his friends.

He then went to buy burgers, a kebab and chips, with CCTV captured at 01:20 BST showing him clutching a takeaway as he staggered through the town.

After sleeping in a shop doorway for an hour, Corrie disappeared from the view of cameras on Brentgovel Street at 03:25 into an area known as the Horseshoe. He was never seen again.

What followed was a huge search and rescue mission, which cost Suffolk Police more than £2m , captivated the country and fuelled conspiracy theorists.

It culminated in the excavation of a landfill site at Milton, Cambridgeshire, which lasted several months but found nothing.

On 22 March 2022, after nearly six years of speculation, inquest jurors provided an explanation for Corrie's disappearance .

Delivering a narrative conclusion they said he died at about 04:20 BST as a result of "compression asphyxia in association with multiple injuries".

These injuries, they ruled, were suffered after Corrie, from Dunfermline, Fife, had climbed into a commercial waste bin - something he had used before as somewhere to sleep - before it was tipped into a refuse truck.

During the inquest, Suffolk Coroner's Court heard that 30 tonnes of force was exerted during each compaction cycle in the back of a bin lorry and so the chances of someone surviving were "slim ".

'We have a mini Corrie to remind us of him'

While Nicola, a former Police Scotland sergeant, accepts the final judgement, she says only she could truly decide when she could achieve a sense of closure.

"No one thing externally can give me closure. The only thing that can give me closure is myself saying, have I done everything I can?" she says.

Corrie's nine-year-old daughter Ellie, who was born nine months after he went missing , has also been a blessing, Nicola says.

She adds her son lives on through her "lovely, happy and well-behaved" granddaughter.

"She's just like her dad, it's frightening; she looks so much like him, she's got his mannerisms, she's adorable, athletic, sporty," she says.

"It's so lovely having a little mini Corrie to remind us of him, she is the very best of him, and she's a very lucky little girl, in some respects, with the family that she's got.

"It is fantastic having Ellie in our lives - it genuinely is just a little bit of Corrie."

Nicola says Corrie's family are doing "so many little things" to ensure Ellie is constantly reminded of her dad in the best and most "positive way".

They include going to the Cenotaph in London on Remembrance Day every year and enjoying her dad's favourite activities, such as going to watch Wicked the Musical.

One day, Nicola adds, Ellie will be presented with a special gift that once belonged to her car-loving dad Corrie.

"[Corrie's brother] Darroch got his MG car that was on the base and spent a lot of time trying to get the car back on the road again," adds Nicola, who lives in Scotland.

"The car is going to Ellie - whether it will still be running when she can drive, I do not know, but she's going to be the one that has his car.

"She's got a father figure, who is her dad, and he's fantastic, but she also knows exactly who Corrie is and who Corrie's family are," she says.

Police officers apologised 'with tears in their eyes'

In the years that followed Corrie's disappearance, Nicola and his family were critical of Suffolk Police and how it had initially handled the investigation.

They accused the force of failing to follow up lines of inquiry, withholding information from the family and ruling out third party involvement early on.

After the inquest, however, Nicola said officers "genuinely privately apologised to each and every" member of the family with "tears in their eyes" and later stated the police "got it right".

The same cannot be said, she claimed, for Biffa, the waste management company which owned the bin in which it was believed Corrie found himself.

It initially told police the weight of the bin was 11kg (1st 10lbs), and therefore not heavy enough to contain a person , but it was later recorded as 116kg (18st 3lbs).

One of the recommendations that came out of the inquest was that locks should be put on large public bins to prevent anybody from being able to get into them.

"My biggest regret and the thing that causes us the longest lasting distress is Biffa and how they made us feel at the time with what they did and didn't do," she said.

"But more importantly, they've not learned their lessons - every time I come to Bury St Edmunds the bins behind where he went missing are still unlocked.

"Is it possible he went in the back of a bin and ended up in the landfill? Because of Biffa, we will never know what happened to Corrie and that upsets me."

Suffolk Police said its thoughts were with Corrie's family and friends on the 10th anniversary of his disappearance.

"As we have explained previously, the active inquiry into Corrie Mckeague's disappearance is now closed," a spokesperson said.

"Unless any new, realistic and credible information becomes available then the investigation remains complete.

"Currently, there remains no information available that changes the status of the investigation."

The RAF said its "thoughts and sympathies" remained with the "family, friends and colleagues of Corrie Mckeague".

Biffa issued a statement that said the safety of the public and employees remained its highest priority.

"Our teams undertake regular training and refresher programmes, and we have introduced additional warning signage on bins to discourage people from entering them," it said.

"While no action can undo the tragedy experienced by Corrie's family, we remain committed to learning from the findings of the inquest and working collaboratively across the waste management sector to improve safety."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An NIA court in Delhi Wednesday granted bail to six Ukrainian nationals arrested in March this year for allegedly running a training camp for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An NIA court in Delhi Wednesday granted bail to six Ukrainian nationals arrested in March this year for allegedly running a training camp for ethnic armed rebels in India and Myanmar.The court, which ordered their release on a cash bond of Rs 1 lakh each, also discharged them from offences under the Immigration and Foreigners Act following after the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO), which deals with the immigration matters involving foreign nationals, settled the offences on payment of a penalty of Rs 5.5 lakh each.The offences, which pertained to illegal entry and visa violations, are compoundable at the level of the FRRO.Special judge Prashant Sharma granted them default bail on grounds of parity with their American co-accused Matthew Aaron Van Dyke.While granting bail to Dyke on Sept 18, the judge had dismissed the NIA’s opposition, observing that even if the probe was far from over, “at this stage it cannot be concluded that applicant/ accused Matthew Aaron Vandyke is not entitled for default bail”.Default bail is provisioned in the UAPA if the probe agency doesn’t file charge sheet containing offences under the anti-terror law with 180 days of arresting the accused. Following this, the court had directed that the other six accused could also seek default bail.Earlier this month, the agency filed a charge sheet which did not mention provisions of the UAPA, 1967, which was invoked in the initial FIR.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Chitu: "La noche de Radio Marca fue una petición correspondida"
articles.standfirst: Carlos Vicente, nuevo presentador de 'Otra Ronda', primer invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.summary: Carlos Vicente, nuevo presentador de 'Otra Ronda' en las noches de Radio Marca, primer invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.body: Hablamos con Chitu, la nueva voz de Radio Marca en sus noches. El de Almagro siempre fue más de trasnochar que de madrugar... ahora tiene excusa: ‘Otra Ronda’. Un programa con el que aspira a todo en el ‘prime time’ de la radio deportiva española. PREGUNTA: ¿Cómo empezó en esto del periodismo? RESPUESTA: Depende de dónde quieras que lo remonte. Lo primero fue llevarme un bloc de notas al bar cuando veía los partidos con mi padre y ponerle nota a los jugadores. Después descubrí que de esto se podía hacer una profesión. Me vine a estudiar a Madrid, desde Almagro, a la Universidad Complutense, donde hay un punto de inflexión bastante claro: un grupo de chavales que estábamos en la Complu hicimos una web, se llamaba Capital Deporte, y a raíz de ahí empezamos a hacer pinitos. La cosa se fue de madre cuando nos dieron acreditaciones para el Bernabéu. P: Cuando estaba con su padre poniendo notas a jugadores, ¿soñaba con llegar hasta donde ha llegado? R: Sí, soy un tío súper vocacional en esto. No lo hago por el dinero, ni por la fama, aunque ahora me estoy acostumbrando a ella. Esto es lo que me mueve, lo que me impulsa, lo que hace que me quede hasta las dos, tres, cuatro de la mañana en una redacción, viniendo a primera hora, o que haya estado 7 años madrugando, viniendo a las cinco y media. P: De esos inicios, ¿hay algún momento que recuerde con especial cariño? R: Lo de la final de Milán no está mal. Eran dos equipos de Madrid, y no pensábamos que la UEFA nos iba a dar la acreditación con nuestra web, pero ahí estuvimos. Me hice el camino Madrid-Milán en autobús: 31 horas de ida, 28 de vuelta, controles en Francia con los gendarmes, un pastor alemán lamiéndome la cara... P: Después de esas aventuras, ¿cómo y cuándo llega Marca? R: Llego después de una beca de dos meses en la Cadena Cope, en el verano de 2016. Después me fui con mi madre a Fuengirola, tras currarme todo el año de universidad con Capital Deporte y todo el verano con la Cope. Nada más desempacar la maleta en el hotel, me llamó un número largo: era Unidad Editorial, preguntando si podía empezar pasado mañana. Le pedí permiso a mi madre y ella soltó un sí absoluto con solo un 0,1% de resignación, porque ya teníamos el hotel pagado y lo perdimos, pero ambos sabíamos que era el camino. Así empecé de prácticas en Radio Marca. P: ¿Cómo recuerda esas primeras prácticas, el primer día, la primera vez que estuvo en antena? R: A pesar de haber hecho prácticas en Cope, iba un poco perdido. La radio me imponía un respeto que me sigue imponiendo, y por entonces se podía llamar incluso miedo. Los primeros días fueron complicados: me acuerdo de los primeros partidos de baloncesto por pasos, donde tenía que hablar al final de cada cuarto. Tenía que sostener el micrófono con las dos manos porque con una me temblaba mucho. Con el tiempo me fui adaptando, notaba que cada día mejoraba un poco. P: ¿De dónde nace su relación tan especial con la música? R: Yo entiendo en esta vida de tres cosas: de futbolistas, de DJs y de (suena un pitido). Son aficiones que uno tiene y que al final consigue meter en su trabajo. Cuando vi que se podía abrir una rendija en ese aspecto, me gustó bastante. P: ¿Cómo llegó exactamente? R: No fue premeditado. Ya llevaba un tiempo en la radio y tenía la libertad para interesarme por ciertos temas. Me enteré de que Manuel Turizo, un artista al que llevo tatuada una canción suya, venía a España concediendo entrevistas a medios musicales y de juventud. Entré en la web de contacto de Manuel Turizo y puse un mail diciendo que era de Radio Marca y que me gustaría entrevistarle, aunque no sabía en qué programa lo colaría. La cosa trascendió y fue creciendo. Al final propuse un programa de música llamado 'El Caserío', que esta semana cumple 100 programas. P: Hay otra relación que llama la atención: su vínculo tan estrecho con Luis de la Fuente. ¿Cómo nace esa amistad? R: Nace de cuando pido hacer las categorías inferiores de la selección española. Lo pido justo cuando Luis está transitando de la sub-19 a la sub-21 y un día me toca entrevistarle: fue un flechazo. El día de la entrevista falló todo lo técnico a la hora de grabar, y mientras yo intentaba reenganchar el cacharro, acabamos pasando 20 minutos y tomándonos un refresco juntos. Ahí comprendimos que nos hacíamos gracia mutuamente, que teníamos buena vibra. Luis no era entonces la superestrella que es ahora, pero sigue siendo la misma persona. Desde entonces, cada Nochevieja es él quien me llama para felicitar el año a mí y a mi familia, habla con mis padres, y poco a poco hemos desarrollado un sentimiento. P: En todo este tiempo, desde que llega a Marca, ¿cuál es el mejor momento que ha vivido? R: Venimos de una final del Mundial, así que no podría decir otra cosa que estar en Nueva York cumpliendo el sueño de todo niño. Estaba con mi radio, con Radio Marca, con la que llevo 10 años trabajando y viviendo, porque al final mi vida es la radio; y estaba la España de Luis de la Fuente, que completaba la amalgama y que también llevo tatuado. Es el momento donde confluye todo y donde no podía pedir nada más. P: ¿Qué opinó Luis cuando le vio el tatuaje? R: Le gustó un montón, le flipó. No fue una sorpresa total porque, cuando vino a Marca, yo se lo avisé con la esperanza de que me dijera "no hace falta, Carlos", pero me dijo que le encantaba la idea y que le pasara el diseño. Le encantó el diseño, así que fui adelante, gustoso de hacerlo. P: Ha tenido una trayectoria en Radio Marca de muchos años madrugando, pero ahora está trasnochando. ¿Cómo llega 'Otra Ronda'? R: Llega porque buscaba crecer, y por primera vez en 10 años me planteé que, si no podía seguir creciendo en Marca, crecería en otro lado. Fue una petición que fue correspondida; no diría que fue un ultimátum, pero sí algo muy a tener en cuenta de cara a mi futuro. Quería hacer la noche y quería cerrar mi etapa junto a Raúl Varela por las mañanas. Él es, como digo siempre, lo más parecido a un padre que tengo aquí en Madrid, pero necesitaba hacer otra cosa en la radio y solo veía la noche como opción. P: ¿Cómo le gustaría ver al Chitu del futuro? R: Espero seguir siendo buena persona y seguir siendo buen periodista; tengo mis cosas, no soy perfecto, puedo equivocarme. Mi abuelo, antes de morirse, repetía como una letanía que fuera buena gente y trabajador; incluso en sus últimos años, cuando ya la edad le hacía mella y cortaba el discurso, seguía diciéndome eso cada vez que volvía a Almagro. No lo llevo tatuado, pero sí muy presente en el día a día. ¿Su olor favorito? Vainilla. ¿El insulto que más usa? Reventado. ¿Y la mentira? La piadosa, la que evita una verdad que haga más daño. ¿Qué es lo que más vergüenza ajena le da? Mis amigos cuando ligan; son malísimos. ¿Un miedo absurdo? Las cucarachas. ¿El contacto más famoso de su agenda? El de Karim Benzema.

articles.title: Gyanesh Kumar should be criminally prosecuted for 'treason': Priyanka Gandhi on SIR row
articles.summary: Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra on Thursday slammed the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, alleging that he should be \"criminally prosecuted\" if
articles.body: Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra on Thursday slammed the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, alleging that he should be "criminally prosecuted" if found responsible for "tampering with electoral rolls and deleting voters' names."Her remarks came a day after The Indian Express published a report claiming that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Speaking to reporters in Wayanad, Kerala, Priyanka Gandhi said, "Anybody who plays around with the process, the democratic process of our elections is committing treason against this nation. That is our very clear stand. I do not think anybody in that position should have legal protection in the way that he has. The Chief Election Commissioner has. If they have done illegal acts because tampering with the voters' rolls, deleting, I believe, 13 crore voters is a criminal act against democracy, against the Constitution and against the nation.""Since criminal acts fall under a particular law, and people are usually tried and prosecuted for doing those criminal acts, I do not see why the Election Commissioner has to have any protection against it," the Congress MP said."If he has done an illegal act, he has been fully aware that this is happening under his nose. His colleagues have brought it to his attention. He has ignored it and intentionally allowed an unfair election to take place. He should be criminally prosecuted just like any other criminal, and he should be tried for treason. This is my very clear stand," she added.Earlier on Wednesday, Priyanka Gandhi had also called the issue "an extremely serious" one for democracy."This is an extremely serious issue for our democracy. If there are no elections, then where is democracy? If elections are unfair and rigged in any manner, then the Election Commission is assisting in that. If the Election Commissioner is not only aware of it but also allowing it to happen, then it is a very serious assault on democracy. It is an act of treason," she said.'Electoral process completely tainted': CongCongress leader Jairam Ramesh also launched a fresh attack on Gyanesh Kumar , alleging irregularities in the ECINet software and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Ramesh said a series of reports had raised serious questions over the functioning of the poll panel and alleged that the electoral process had been "completely compromised and tainted".He said, "Yesterday, sensational revelations in a major national daily brought to light that the CEC has completely undermined the integrity, reliability, and competence of the Election Commission. This morning, another report in this series has emerged."Ramesh alleged that Goa's chief electoral officer (CEO) wrote to the ECI eight times in seven days seeking the reinstatement of valid voters whose names had been removed by the ECINet software. He said Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) had confirmed that the voters were valid, but their emails were ignored and the names were removed.He also stated that the process for adding new voters through Form 6 had been made more difficult and claimed that Gen Z was being "deliberately targeted" to exclude young voters from electoral rolls.Ramesh said the latest allegations reinforced what leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi had been saying for nearly two years, referring to the results of the Haryana and Maharashtra assembly elections."The electoral process has been completely compromised and tainted. This is the implementation of the Method of Disenfranchising Indians (MODI) by Gyanesh Kumar," Ramesh said.He also called for the CEC's resignation, saying, "If there is even a shred of decency and ethics left in CEC Gyanesh Kumar, his first step should be to immediately resign from his position. After that, the Prime Minister and Home Minister will be held accountable for their nefarious designs."'Justice will be served': RahulCongress leader Rahul Gandhi also took to X, stating that, "The enemies of the Constitution have been exposed. Justice will be served."Earlier on Wednesday, Rahul described "vote chori" as a "crime against the Indian people" and an attack on the Constitution.In a post on X, Rahul Gandhi said, "Vote chori is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served."In a video, he also addressed the Election Commission and election officials, saying, "I am clearly telling the Election Commission and election officers: What you are doing is wrong. This is treason; it is against the nation. Do not forget this. The time will come! We will catch you! You will not be spared."'All actions have been in accordance': ECAccording to the media report, Election Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had objected at least 14 times to decisions taken in the Commission's name without their knowledge or approval. The reported objections covered issues including voter registration and deletion, changes to Form 6 and the handling of the electoral-roll database.The ECI rejected the suggestion that the reported objections amounted to a division within the Commission. ECI officials said all decisions, including those related to SIR, were taken unanimously with the approval of all three commissioners.In a statement, the poll panel said, "The ECI is a constitutional body that functions under the strict mandate of Article 324 of the Constitution, statutory rules and established institutional conventions. The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour. All actions of ECI have been in accordance with laws and instructions of the Commission. All official orders, decisions and administrative directions issued by the Commission carry full legal sanctions and follow established statutory procedures."The Commission further said, "Any operational queries or inputs raised by Commission members during draft stages are part of standard administrative practice aimed at safeguarding voter rights. The suggestions given by the Commissioners were for further improving the electoral processes," adding that differing views and observations were a normal part of institutional deliberations.'All three Commissioners were unanimous': BJPBJP national spokesperson and MP Sambit Patra earlier defended the functioning of the Election Commission, saying discussions among the three commissioners were part of the democratic process."Look at the situation: if the three Election Commissioners do not communicate with each other, if there is no exchange of views or consultation, and they simply agree to everything, then the opposition parties claim it is a dictatorship. They say this government appointed these three commissioners; they just say yes. Now, there have been 14 instances of correspondence among the three of them, official deliberations, as far as we gather from the media. It is not as if the Bharatiya Janata Party goes and reads these letters; rather, reports in the media indicate that official deliberations took place among the three, which is a sign of a healthy democracy," he said."I would say that today, all the opposition parties have fallen into a trap, the trap of claiming that the Election Commission and the government were acting dictatorially. On the contrary, I would say this is pure democracy. Deliberations are taking place, and the Election Commission has stated very clearly in the very first paragraph of its document that, following all official democratic deliberations, the final outcome, the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), was achieved with unanimity," Patra said."In other words, all three Commissioners were unanimous; there was no difference of opinion or dissent among them," he added.Meanwhile, ECI sources maintained that all decisions taken by the poll panel, including those related to SIR, were unanimous and had the approval of both Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent
articles.summary: Her heavy metal performance trumped nine other finalists, including magicians and even a robot crew.
articles.body:
Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show.

For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.

Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew.

Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".

Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views.

On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band.

Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (£755,000).

"I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her.

The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC.

Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements.

But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory.

"History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook.

"Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win.

"What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday.

"She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream."

According to Nene, she started playing the guitar when she was seven years old and harboured dreams of becoming a touring musician.

In her hometown of Phuket, a tourist hub known for its beaches and seaside resorts, Nene was known to busk at Naka Weekend Market.

Piyarat Na Songkhla, 43, tour guide in Phuket, tells the BBC that he has seen Nene Royal perform since she was young.

"She's so adorable," he says. "I feel so elated and happy for her. It's unbelievable that she has gone this far. So proud of her."

The Facebook account of Naka Weekend Market posted a tribute to Nene after her victory.

"Everyone at Naka Market is so proud to see you shine on one of the biggest stages in the world," its post reads.

"Your talent, heart, and courage have inspired so many people, and this victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream."

Kajonkiet International School in Phuket, where Nene studies, also congratulated her on the win.

"We are so proud of you," reads a Facebook post from the school, which posted a video of its students and staff gathering to watch Nene's final performance, screaming and chanting her name.

articles.title: From a rented room and a missed Cambridge dream to Padma Shri: How Anand Kumar built Super 30 and changed the lives of underprivileged IIT aspirants through free education and hope
articles.summary: What began as a small mathematics initiative in Patna eventually became one of India’s best-known education stories.
articles.body: What began as a small mathematics initiative in Patna eventually became one of India’s best-known education stories. Anand Kumar started teaching mathematics in 1992 through the Ramanujan School of Mathematics, aiming to make quality learning accessible to students. His own struggles with money later shaped the direction of his work, leading him to focus increasingly on talented students from economically weaker families. In 2023, his contribution to education was recognised with the Padma Shri in the Literature and Education category.A mathematics dream that began in PatnaAnand Kumar developed a strong interest in mathematics from an early age. While pursuing his graduation in Patna, he began a mathematics club in 1992, which later became known as the Ramanujan School of Mathematics. According to the institute's account of his journey, the programme initially offered free mathematics training to anyone interested in learning the subject. The initiative gradually grew as more students became interested. What started as a modest effort eventually became a larger coaching programme. Kumar began training students for competitive examinations and kept the fees low for those who could afford them. Students facing severe financial difficulties were allowed to study without paying.His work was closely connected to his own experience of financial hardship. In 1994, Kumar received an opportunity to pursue higher education at the University of Cambridge. However, he could not take up the opportunity because his family could not afford the costs involved. The setback became an important turning point in his life. Instead of allowing the lost opportunity to end his academic ambitions, Kumar began thinking about other students who faced similar barriers. His experience convinced him that talent alone was not enough when a family could not afford quality education and coaching.How the Super 30 idea took shapeKumar continued developing the Ramanujan School of Mathematics and eventually turned his attention towards students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds who wanted to enter India's premier technical institutions. This effort led to Super 30, the programme for which he became widely known. The initiative selected a group of talented students from financially disadvantaged backgrounds and provided them with intensive preparation for the IIT-JEE, along with food and accommodation. The aim was to remove the financial barriers that could otherwise prevent capable students from pursuing their ambitions. The programme's official history says Kumar decided to develop a more focused initiative for poor but meritorious students, eventually creating Super 30 with his brother Pranav Kumar.Over the years, the programme attracted national and international attention because of the achievements of its students. Kumar's work was also recognised by the Limca Book of Records for his contribution to helping economically disadvantaged students prepare for the IIT-JEE. His approach was built around a straightforward belief: a student's financial circumstances should not decide how far their talent can take them.From a missed Cambridge opportunity to national recognitionThe story of Anand Kumar is therefore not simply about the success of Super 30. It is also about how a personal setback was transformed into an educational mission. The opportunity to study at Cambridge was one he could not afford to pursue. Years later, however, his work helped other students access opportunities that might otherwise have remained beyond their reach. The Government of India's Padma Awards records describe Kumar as a grassroots educator from Bihar known for providing free coaching to underprivileged children preparing for national examinations. He was selected for the Padma Shri in 2023 under Literature and Education.President Droupadi Murmu formally presented him the Padma Shri at a civil investiture ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan in April 2023. From teaching mathematics through a small initiative in Patna to building Super 30 and receiving one of India's highest civilian honours, Kumar's journey shows how education can become more than a profession. articles.body: A Sita Airlines aircraft carrying 16 people suffered a runway mishap while landing at Juphal Airport in Dolpa district of Nepal’s Karnali Province on Thursday after its rear right wheel came off, officials said.According to PTI, the aircraft was carrying 13 passengers and three crew members, including seven foreign nationals, when the rear right wheel came off during landing. The aircraft had taken off from Nepalgunj for Dolpa and came to a halt on the runway at around 8:25 am local time.“The small aircraft carrying 13 passengers and three crew members met with an accident right on the runway after its rear right tyre came off,” Anil Raj Giri, deputy superintendent of police at the District Police Office in Dolpa, told PTI.The pilot immediately switched off the engine after the incident, preventing any further mishap. All 16 people on board were safe, while the aircraft suffered no major structural damage, PTI reported.However, the aircraft remained stranded on the runway, forcing authorities to suspend all flight operations at Juphal Airport. A Nepali Army aircraft approaching the airport was also forced to turn back.According to PTI, repair work on the runway is underway, with authorities arranging to fly technicians by helicopter to clear the aircraft and restore normal flight operations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hot chilli legacy of summer heatwave
articles.summary: An amateur gardener from Stoke Gifford says he has produced a bumper crop of chillies.
articles.body:
An amateur gardener has produced a bumper crop of chillies - boosted by the scorching hot summer.

Jeremy Crumb from Stoke Gifford near Bristol only began growing the South American plants a few years ago but now tends dozens of varieties in his small back garden.

He said: "What's been very interesting this year, is normally it's the plants in the greenhouse that flourish, but because of the very hot summer even the ones outside are healthy and absolutely stacked out with fruit.

"I've been on a mission to produce the biggest, healthiest chilli plants I can - it's really addictive and there's so many different varieties, they've all got these little unique nuances to them."

Among the varieties he grows are familiar chillies - such as Habanero, Bird's Eye, Jalapeno and Peri Peri - alongside more exotic choices such as Turtle Claw, Volcano and Paper Lantern.

He has produced so many this year that he's had to invest in a dehydrator.

He says: "It's like a little oven and it dehydrates them at 50C (122F). I had to get it because I just had so many chillies and I can only freeze or give so many away.

"I also ferment them and turn them into sauces, seasonings and rubs."

Crumb says the hottest chilli he has grown this year is the Caramel Scorpion which, like the Carolina Reaper, is measured at around 1.6 million Scovilles - the scale on which the heat of a chilli pepper is recorded.

He says: "They've got really interesting sort of pumpkin-shaped fruits and they're ridiculously hot, if you ate one it would be very uncomfortable and it would give you a bad stomach ache.

"But I think people focus on the heat and they don't understand that each chilli - if you get past the heat - has a distinctive flavour - and it's a flavour that you perhaps haven't tasted before and can't replicate with any other fruit."

Crumb never forgets about the potential danger of handling chillies.

He says: "Even if you're chopping them up or processing them, you need to wear gloves or you'll forget what you've touched."

He adds that even after washing your hands, there will still be capsaicin, the oil from the middle of the chilli, on them.

However, he says that several garden visitors have happily chomped on his crop, adding: "Birds don't have capsaicin receptors, neither do slugs.

"So that part of our mouth that can detect the spice, those animals just don't have.

"And because of that, they are happy to eat as many as they like."

articles.title: IIT-Bombay suicide case: Sahil Wakode's father detained on way to campus to begin hunger strike
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police on Thursday detained Ravindra Wakode in Bhandup while he was travelling to IIT-Bombay’s Powai campus to begin a hunger strike
articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police on Thursday detained Ravindra Wakode in Bhandup while he was travelling to IIT-Bombay’s Powai campus to begin a hunger strike following the death of his son, second-year student Sahil Wakode.Wakode said he wanted to undertake the hunger strike for his son, who died by suicide on September 18.His planned protest came as Mumbai Youth Congress and NSUI workers staged a demonstration outside the IIT-Bombay campus in Powai demanding a fast-track inquiry and justice for Sahil.Police also detained several protesting NSUI-Congress workers and tightened security around the campus.CCTV cameras recorded Sahil's movementAccording to the preliminary findings of the Mumbai Police Crime Branch, CCTV cameras recorded Sahil’s movements inside the examination hall between 12.30pm and 12.45pm on September 18.Police said that with about 15 minutes remaining for the examination, Sahil was seen bending down to look at something kept in his pocket. A professor then questioned him and took him aside, away from the other students, according to the Crime Branch."After leaving the examination hall, Sahil moved across the campus. He reached his hostel room at approximately 1.25pm. He did not step out of the room thereafter," a Crime Branch official said.The investigation is being conducted by an assistant commissioner of police under the supervision of the deputy commissioner of police, Detection-I, Crime Branch. Police have appealed to people not to speculate or draw premature conclusions.IIT-Bombay has also formed a 10-member committee to examine the circumstances surrounding Sahil’s death. Professor Doolla has been relieved of his administrative responsibilities and sent on leave pending the inquiry.'Most upright professors that we have'Several current and former IIT-Bombay colleagues have backed Doolla and objected to the suspension of his deanship.Sharad Kumar Saraf, a former chairman of the institute’s Board of Governors, said he believed Doolla was innocent and that there was no evidence of caste-based discrimination against him."I have known Professor Doolla. During my tenure as Chairman of the Board of Governors of IIT, he was the Dean of Students' Affairs, one of the most upright professors that we have," Saraf said.He also disputed the suggestion that caste had been discussed during the examination incident, saying the issue was raised by Sahil’s family after his death.Sahil, a second-year BTech student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering, died by suicide on September 18.His family has alleged harassment and caste-based discrimination. articles.title: Sam Altman-backed Praxis plans $1 billion AI-powered town in Uruguay; first residents expected in mid-2027 with homes, resorts and cultural spaces for the AI era
articles.summary: Praxis, a technology-focused community backed by Apollo Projects, a fund associated with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, has selected Uruguay for its first
articles.body: Praxis, a technology-focused community backed by Apollo Projects, a fund associated with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, has selected Uruguay for its first physical development. The project involves a projected investment of about $1 billion in the +Colonia development near Colonia del Sacramento. The first Praxis residents are expected to arrive around mid-2027, while construction of the larger community continues over the following years. Plans include private residences, a resort and spaces for art, music and other cultural activities. Praxis presents the project as an experiment in how communities could live and organise in a future shaped by artificial intelligence.Sam Altman-backed Praxis selects Uruguay for its $1 billion AI-powered townAfter searching for a location for about two years, Praxis chose +Colonia, a waterfront urban development near Colonia del Sacramento, as the home of its first physical community. The location offers access to the Río de la Plata and is close to both Montevideo and Buenos Aires. Eduardo Bastitta, founder of +Colonia, has described the partnership as an opportunity to bring together technology, entrepreneurship and new forms of community living.Praxis says its wider online community has more than 150,000 members, including entrepreneurs, investors and people working in technology and artificial intelligence. About 2,700 members have expressed interest in moving to or investing in the Uruguay project. Rather than creating a completely new city on undeveloped land, Praxis is establishing its community within the existing +Colonia development, where construction is already underway.$1 billion investment planned over several yearsThe $1 billion figure attached to the project represents projected investment, rather than money already spent on construction. According to El País and El Observador, the initial Praxis area is expected to cover approximately 350,000 square metres, or roughly 20% of the planned +Colonia urbanisation.Much of the projected spending is expected to be connected to residences and other facilities that Praxis members will purchase or develop. The land transaction is also expected to progress in stages. El País reported that the land sale had not been completed when Praxis announced the project, meaning the full development remains dependent on subsequent agreements, purchases and construction.First residents expected in mid-2027The first members of the Praxis community are expected to arrive at +Colonia around mid-2027, but that date does not represent the completion of the wider project.Instead, early residents are expected to move into buildings already being developed at +Colonia while the dedicated Praxis neighbourhood takes shape. This allows the community to establish a physical presence before the full range of planned facilities is completed.Dryden Brown, Praxis's co-founder and CEO, is also expected to relocate to Uruguay as the project gets underway.Homes, resorts and cultural spaces plannedThe proposed community is designed to combine residential life with hospitality and cultural activities. Praxis plans private residences, a resort and spaces for art and music, alongside studios, galleries and workshops.The company's vision also includes restaurants, nightlife venues, gardens, public squares, a waterfront promenade and a beach club. Photography, film and music production spaces are also planned, while fellowship programmes could bring artists, musicians, designers, writers and founders to the community.Concept images released by Praxis show minimalist buildings with large glass openings, landscaped areas and pools overlooking the waterfront. These remain proposed designs and do not guarantee that every structure shown will ultimately be built in the same form.A community designed around the AI eraThe physical development is closely tied to Praxis's broader philosophy about the impact of artificial intelligence. The organisation says it wants to develop new cultural, economic and governance systems for what it describes as a post-AGI world.Its vision is centred on bringing together people involved in technology, entrepreneurship and creative fields and giving them a physical environment in which to live and collaborate as AI changes work and economic activity.However, the currently announced plans do not establish that the town will have AI-controlled utilities, autonomous transport or an AI-run government. The confirmed physical plans focus on housing, hospitality, cultural facilities and community spaces. In this context, the description of the project as “AI-powered” primarily reflects Praxis's technology-driven vision rather than a confirmed specification for all of its infrastructure.Sam Altman's connection to PraxisAltman's connection to the project comes through Apollo Projects, which Uruguayan media identify as a fund associated with the OpenAI CEO and one of Praxis's backers.That connection does not mean Altman personally owns or is directly developing the Uruguay project, nor does it mean OpenAI is building the community. Praxis is led by Brown, who has described the development as a way to explore how people might live, work and find purpose as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential.The involvement of an Altman-associated fund nevertheless places the project within the wider network of technology and AI investment that has emerged around the development of new communities and infrastructure.+Colonia provides the physical foundationPraxis is entering a development that already exists rather than starting with an empty site. +Colonia is being built as a large waterfront community near Colonia del Sacramento, with construction already underway.The existing buildings provide a starting point for Praxis's first residents, while the dedicated neighbourhood can be developed progressively. According to El Observador, the initial Praxis area would account for roughly one-fifth of the broader +Colonia urbanisation.This arrangement also explains why the first residents can arrive in 2027 even though the larger project is expected to take considerably longer to develop.Who is expected to live there?Praxis's wider community includes more than 150,000 people, but only a small portion are currently expected to relocate to Uruguay. Around 2,700 members have indicated interest in moving to or investing in the project.The proposed community is aimed at a mix of entrepreneurs, investors, technology professionals and creative workers. Alongside residential facilities, the planned studios, galleries, restaurants and cultural spaces are intended to encourage interaction between those groups.The result is intended to be less a conventional residential development and more a concentrated community built around technology, business and creative activity.The project remains in its early stagesDespite its ambitious scale and futuristic designs, the Praxis development remains an evolving project. The $1 billion figure is a projection for future investment, while land acquisition and construction are expected to proceed in stages.For now, the most immediate milestone is the planned arrival of the first Praxis residents around mid-2027. The larger neighbourhood, including its homes, resort and cultural facilities, is expected to take shape over the years that follow.If the plans proceed as announced, the Uruguay project will give Praxis its first permanent physical base and turn its vision of an AI-era community from an online experiment into a real-world development.You use AI every day. articles.title: This former Portland school now has a hotel, brewery, movie theater and soaking pool, without losing its classrooms’ old character
articles.summary: Explore the remarkable transformation of Portland's Kennedy School into a vibrant hotel, brewery, movie theater, and soaking pool, all while preserving its historical charm and character. Discover how this 1915 building continues to serve as a community gathering space.
articles.body: The bell at Portland's Kennedy School rang for the last time as an elementary school in 1975, and more than two decades later, the same building reopened with hotel rooms in former classrooms, a movie theater in the old auditorium, a brewery, bars, restaurants and a soaking pool.The building in Northeast Portland dates to 1915, when it opened as Kennedy Elementary School, served generations of local children and also became a community space outside school hours. According to McMenamins' history of the property, the school was used as a public meeting hall, polling place, Red Cross blood-drawing center, weekend playground and even a flood-relief shelter. The school closed at the end of the 1974-75 academic year because of declining enrollment and the condition of the aging building, after which it sat vacant while demolition orders threatened its future.The school nearly disappearedA coalition of neighbors, former students, former PTA presidents and the Portland Development Commission worked to prevent the old school from being demolished. Several ideas were considered for the property before brothers Mike and Brian McMenamin proposed turning it into a new kind of community gathering place.The renovation began in 1997, and the National Trust for Historic Preservation reported that the building needed new plumbing, electrical work, and structural upgrades after years of vacancy. The challenge was to make the building usable again without stripping away the features that made it recognizable as a school. Former classrooms became guest rooms, and some retained their original chalkboards and cloakrooms. Historic architectural details were restored, and artwork was added throughout the building.The National Trust noted that the school reopened in October 1997 with its old chalkboards still in place, restored 1915 bas-relief panels, and even the small drinking fountains that were designed for children. Much of the building's former layout remained visible, even as the rooms were given entirely different uses.From classrooms to hotel roomsToday, McMenamins lists 57 guest rooms at the Kennedy School, with some occupying former classrooms, while also including a restaurant, several small bars, a movie theater, a brewery, a gift shop and the soaking pool. The soaking pool occupies a private courtyard that was formerly associated with the teachers' lounge. Hotel guests have access as part of their stay, while members of the public can also use it during designated hours for a fee.The building's artwork and interior details draw heavily on the school's past, while some spaces continue to suggest their original purpose. A visitor can move from a room that was once a classroom to a bar, theater, or dining space without leaving the same 1915 structure. That is also why the Kennedy School is different from a typical adaptive-reuse project, since the building was not simply preserved as a museum, nor was its original identity completely replaced by a new commercial use.The Oregon Encyclopedia notes that the Kennedy School was among the McMenamins projects that transformed older buildings into places that combined hospitality, entertainment and community uses. The former elementary school became part of that wider approach to preserving older Portland structures by giving them new functions. The property also retained a role as a gathering place for the neighborhood, much as the school had done before its closure.The school opened in 1915, spent decades serving children and the surrounding community, closed in 1975 and remained vacant for about 17 years before its 1997 reopening. The principal's original bell was rung on October 22, 1997, which marked the building's second life as McMenamins Kennedy School. More than a century after the school building opened, its classrooms are no longer filled with students, but some, however, still have their chalkboards. The old auditorium shows movies, the former school grounds contain gardens and courtyards, and the property now accommodates overnight guests alongside diners, drinkers and moviegoers.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1907, an American performer strapped on water shoes and walked 1,600 miles down two rivers; 40 days later, he stepped ashore in New Orleans
articles.summary: In 1907, Charles W. Oldrieve embarked on an extraordinary challenge, walking 1,600 miles on water down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers in just 40 days. This feat, involving oversized wooden shoes, captivated audiences and marked a remarkable chapter in performance history, ending tragically. Read about his journey, the challenges he faced, and his lasting legacy.
articles.body: Charles W. Oldrieve stepped into the Ohio River at Cincinnati on January 1, 1907, and wore a pair of oversized wooden shoes that looked more like tiny canoes than footwear. He had set himself a 40-day challenge of travelling down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers and reaching New Orleans. The route covered nearly 1,600 miles, which Oldrieve completed on February 10, after arriving in New Orleans about an hour ahead of the deadline. A contemporary newspaper report said that he covered the distance in 40 days, and finished 45 minutes inside the agreed limit.Oldrieve was a former tightrope performer from Boston who had spent years developing his method of walking on water. His shoes were made from wood and designed to float, were roughly four to four-and-a-half feet long and fitted with fins underneath that helped him push against the water as he moved forward. The shoes provided flotation while the fins gave him traction. Without the fins, he could float but would struggle to make forward progress.He had been practicing for yearsIn 1888, at age 20, he walked more than 150 miles down the Hudson River from Albany to Manhattan, and by the early 1900s, he could walk forward and backward in his shoes and had learned to turn around on the water. The Smithsonian Magazine reported that Oldrieve had once dreamed of walking across the English Channel and even the Atlantic. Those plans never happened, but his river journey became his longest documented water-walking expedition. During the 1907 expedition, Oldrieve was accompanied by a small gas-powered support boat, while his wife, Caroline, followed in a rowboat. Crowds gathered along the rivers as he passed through towns.He could reportedly reach about five miles per hour at his fastest, although he estimated his average speed at closer to two miles per hour. The shoes themselves weighed around 20 pounds each, and water frequently got inside them despite the thigh-high rubber boots he wore underneath. At Henderson, Kentucky, he was two days behind schedule, and eventually recovered the lost time after reaching the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois. The journey became more difficult as he continued south, as Oldrieve developed back pain and suffered chills and a high fever, but continued toward New Orleans.The final miles nearly ended the journeyOldrieve was several days into the final stretch and believed he could finish without difficulty, by the time Oldrieve reached Baton Rouge on February 6. The lower Mississippi River carried heavy commercial traffic, and Oldrieve was navigating the water on a pair of floating wooden shoes. Near New Orleans, he was nearly swept underneath a barge and had to be rescued by people who were aboard the vessel. He nevertheless reached New Orleans on February 10, after completing the nearly 1,600-mile journey within the 40-day target. Contemporary accounts reported that he finished less than an hour before the deadline.Oldrieve and Caroline continued travelling and putting on water-based shows after the river journey, and their performances combined his water-walking act with staged effects and demonstrations. During a July 4 performance in Greenwood, Mississippi, Caroline was badly burned while setting off explosives used in the act, and she died from her injuries several days later. Oldrieve was later told that she would recover, but learned of her death while travelling to another performance. Smithsonian Magazine reports that he subsequently died by suicide after drinking chloroform.Oldrieve's 1907 river crossing nevertheless remained the feat that was most closely associated with his name. A historical account in Memphis Magazine describes how the performer spent years developing his cedar water shoes and built a reputation as the “Human Water Spider.”His equipment was simple by modern standards, with wooden shoes, rubber boots, a support boat and a rowboat beside him. But the combination allowed Oldrieve to travel from Cincinnati to New Orleans on the surface of two major American rivers in 40 days, having completed a journey that had begun as one of his most ambitious performance challenges.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Indian Ocean and beyond’: Iran warns war can spread further if US launches fresh attacks
articles.summary: Iran on Thursday warned that any renewed US or Israeli attack could see the conflict expand from the Persian Gulf and Red Sea into the Indian Ocean and
articles.body: Iran on Thursday warned that any renewed US or Israeli attack could see the conflict expand from the Persian Gulf and Red Sea into the Indian Ocean and potentially beyond, signalling a possible widening of the maritime theatre if hostilities resume.Major-General Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, issued the warning in a video released by Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, as cited Al Jazeera. “Since the conflict has spread from the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, it is possible that – in response to more war – the front will expand even further, reaching the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond,” Safavi said.Safavi also said that Iran's armed forces had prepared for a worst-case scenario in the event of renewed US-Israeli attacks, suggesting Tehran was preparing for a conflict that could extend beyond its immediate waters. He further warned that a new front could emerge around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, while praising Yemen's Houthis for their role in the region.“I must state here that if the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait may open up before their very eyes,” Safavi added.Safavi had also warned in a telvised interview that Iran was monitoring US naval activity across the region, including in the Indian Ocean. “In the maritime domain, whether in the skies over the Persian Gulf or even in the Indian Ocean, we detect with our radar systems the US naval vessels currently in the region…and determine where they are located,” he said.Follow live updates on Iran warThe former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander also said Iran had strengthened its missile, drone and air-defence capabilities and was prepared to conduct both defensive and retaliatory operations.“In the missile, air-defense, and territorial-defense sectors, we have reached a level where, God forbid, if they (American forces) intend to land anywhere in Iran, they will certainly be destroyed,” Safavi said.He said Iran had at least 10 million trained Basij personnel who could defend different parts of the country through a distributed approach and asymmetric warfare.“People are the main pillar of the Islamic Republic’s power and national security,” he said.Also read: Iran warns US of new weapons, targetsIRGC warns of new weapons and targetsSafavi's warning follows separate comments from the IRGC on Monday that any renewed escalation with the United States could bring new weapons, military tactics and targets into the conflict.IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said Iran was prepared for a prolonged confrontation and that its defensive and counteroffensive operations would undergo “significant changes” if hostilities intensified. “Those changes include a shift in the geography of war, and a shift in weapons and military equipment,” Mohebbi told local media. “We will bring new weapons with new capabilities into the battlefield, and the world will be astonished.”Mohebbi also warned that Iran's targets in a renewed phase of the conflict would not necessarily be the same as those targeted previously.“Our targets are also no longer necessarily the same [as the] previous targets. We have new targets that have not yet been struck,” he said.In an interview with Al-Alam News Network, Mohebbi said the IRGC had prepared for a “long-term war”, adding that the conflict could pass through different stages but was not over. He also claimed that the US, Israel and their allies had failed to achieve their objectives, pointing to the Strait of Hormuz and arguing that the US had been unable to reopen the strategic waterway despite its military presence in the region.Iran links Hormuz reopening to US concessionsSafavi separately said reopening the Strait of Hormuz would depend on the lifting of what he described as an illegal US naval blockade and on Washington accepting Iranian conditions.“The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened through US military pressure. It is Iran and Oman that can establish the mechanism for this. We are in contact with the Omanis, although public reporting indicates that the United States is preventing this,” he said.“The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is conditional on [the US’s] accepting Iran’s terms.”Safavi said Iran wanted to establish a regional security framework with Persian Gulf states without US involvement.“Our objective is to permanently remove the threat to the Iranian people and, together with the countries of the region, establish lasting security and sustainable development in the Persian Gulf without the presence of the United States,” he said.The warnings come as Washington and Tehran remain locked in a tense military and diplomatic standoff. Iran has said it is ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade, while Trump said on September 22 that talks with Tehran were continuing and that he believed a settlement could eventually be reached. Meanwhile, tensions around Hormuz and the Red Sea remain high, with Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthis exerting pressure on key maritime routes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
